opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important open questions right now, and I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, but with some real caveats about what it'll actually take.

The thing that makes me optimistic is that this is exactly how intelligence works in the real world. People don't learn everything up front from a static dataset and then stop. They learn by doing things, seeing what happens, and adjusting. In robotics we've been thinking about this for a long time, because a robot that's deployed is constantly getting experience: it tries to fold the laundry, it fails, and that failure is informative. The data you get from deployment is in some ways much more valuable than the data you get from passively collecting demonstrations, because it's on-distribution. It shows you the mistakes your system actually makes, not the mistakes some other system or person would make.

So for LLMs, the analogous picture is that you have millions of people interacting with these models, and every interaction contains some signal about whether the model did a good job. In principle, that's an enormous source of experience, way more than any curated dataset.

But here's where I'd temper things. The hard part isn't collecting the data. The hard part is the credit assignment and the reward signal. In a lot of deployed settings, you don't really know whether the outcome was good. A user might not come back, or they might accept an answer that was subtly wrong. If you naively optimize on those signals, you get something more like engagement optimization than actual capability improvement. You can end up with models that are better at seeming helpful rather than being helpful. That's the classic reward-hacking problem, and it gets worse the more you optimize.

The second issue is that a lot of what we currently call learning from deployment is really just collecting data and then doing another big offline training run. That's useful, but it's not the same thing as a system that's genuinely improving itself continually. Real continual learning, where the model incorporates new experience without forgetting what it knew and without someone curating everything in between, is still a fairly unsolved problem.

Where I think it gets really interesting is when these models are doing things in the world with clearer outcomes. Coding is a good example: the code runs or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. And of course physical tasks with robots: did the dish get into the dishwasher or not? Those settings give you grounded feedback, and that's where I'd expect a self-improving flywheel to actually spin first. The more an AI system acts as an agent with real consequences rather than just a text predictor answering queries, the more natural this kind of learning becomes.

So my overall view is: yes, this is coming, and I think it's going to be a big deal. But the bottleneck is going to be figuring out good, grounded feedback and good algorithms for learning from your own experience, essentially making reinforcement learning work robustly at scale, rather than just the fact that you have a lot of users.

r001.rationale: The response is cautiously optimistic that deployed LLMs can improve from use, while identifying feedback and learning algorithms as the main bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: It describes collecting deployment data for later offline training, but does not clearly identify a human-mediated process in which people observe deployed behavior and use those observations to change the model.

r003.rationale: It identifies credit assignment and reliable reward signals as central challenges, including whether user interactions and outcomes indicate genuinely good behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most interesting questions right now, and I'll say up front that I'm somewhat skeptical of the strong version of it, but very optimistic about a weaker version.

The strong version is the idea that you deploy a model, it interacts with millions of people, and somehow that interaction data just flows back and makes the model smarter in a kind of closed loop. And the reason I'm skeptical of that is that the thing that's missing is a real signal. When you look at what makes reinforcement learning work, the thing you need is some notion of what counts as success. In robotics, that's actually fairly easy to come by in a lot of cases, because the robot either picked up the cup or it didn't. In a conversation with a language model, what's the reward? A thumbs up? The user came back the next day? Those are extremely weak and often very misleading signals. If you optimize for "the user liked this response," you're going to get sycophancy, you're going to get models that tell people what they want to hear. We've already seen some of that. So the flywheel in that naive form, I think, spins in a direction you don't actually want.

The weaker version, which I think is real and which I'm actually quite excited about, is that deployment generates something more like experience in the RL sense. The model tries things, some of those things have consequences in the world, and if you can observe those consequences, that's genuine information that wasn't in the pretraining data. That's fundamentally different from just scraping more text. Pretraining data is a record of what humans did; experience is a record of what the model did and what happened as a result. And the second thing is what you need to get beyond imitation.

Where this gets interesting is agentic settings, because that's where the outcomes become more observable. If a model is writing code, you can run the code. If it's doing a task that involves some external tool, you often get feedback about whether it worked. So I'd expect the self-improvement story to actually play out first in those domains, where the signal is grounded in something, rather than in open-ended chat.

There's also a subtlety that I think people underestimate, which is that the data a deployed model generates is heavily shaped by what it's already good at. It gets used for the things it does well, so you get a lot of data about those things and very little about the things it's bad at. That's the opposite of what you want from an exploration standpoint. In RL we think about this a lot: the whole challenge is getting the agent to try things that aren't already in its comfort zone. A deployment loop doesn't naturally do that; if anything, it narrows the distribution.

So my overall assessment is: the flywheel is real, but it's not automatic, and it's not free. It requires actually solving the problems we've been working on in RL for a long time, which are figuring out where the reward comes from, how to explore, and how to learn from outcomes that are delayed and noisy. The models give you an incredible starting point, a prior that's far better than anything we had before. But that last piece, the part where the system genuinely gets better from its own actions rather than from more human data, that's still a research problem. I don't think it's been solved just because the models got big.

r001.rationale: The response directly assesses deployed models improving from use, distinguishing a dubious automatic closed loop from a more promising version grounded in observable outcomes.

r002.rationale: It discusses user feedback and interaction data as possible signals, but does not identify an existing human-mediated loop in which people observe deployed behavior and use those observations to change the model.

r003.rationale: It identifies the lack of a reliable success or reward signal as a central obstacle and explains that learning needs consequences grounded in the model’s actions.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential is very large, but there’s a distinction between collecting experience and learning from it. A model being used by millions of people is getting exposed to lots of different situations. That doesn’t automatically mean you have a learning algorithm that can turn those interactions into better behavior.

The key question is: where does the feedback come from? If somebody asks a question and the model gives an answer, it may never find out whether that answer was useful or correct. You could use whether the person seems satisfied, but that’s an imperfect signal. You might learn to give answers that people like rather than answers that help them.

I’m particularly excited about settings where the model can take actions and observe their consequences. If it’s writing code, it can run the code and see whether the tests pass. If it’s carrying out a task on a computer, there may be some way to check whether it accomplished the task. That starts to look much more like the setting we study in reinforcement learning: you try something, you get an outcome, and you use that outcome to improve.

There are still challenges. You need to assign credit over potentially long sequences of actions, and you need to learn from the experience without making the system worse in other ways. But I don’t think there’s a fundamental reason that deployed systems couldn’t improve substantially from use. I just wouldn’t assume that the flywheel happens automatically because you have a lot of users. You need to close the loop between what the system does, whether it worked, and how you train it.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about the potential for deployed systems to improve, but says improvement is not automatic and depends on closing the feedback loop. It does not clearly assess the flywheel as close to working.

r002.rationale: It discusses possible feedback from users and task outcomes, but does not identify an existing human-mediated process in which observations of deployed behavior lead to changes in the model.

r003.rationale: It makes finding useful feedback a key question, notes that answers may lack signals of correctness or usefulness, and describes checking outcomes to guide training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real opportunity there, but the key question is: what is the learning signal? Getting more interactions is not, by itself, the same thing as getting better. If a model gives you an answer and you move on, did it solve your problem? Did you give up? Those can look pretty similar in the data.

The cases where I’d expect this to work best are ones where the system can actually observe the consequences of its actions. If it writes code, it can run that code and see whether the tests pass. If it’s helping with some longer task, ideally it can determine whether the task was completed. Now you have something closer to a reinforcement learning problem: you try something, observe an outcome, and use that experience to improve.

There’s also a distinction between learning during a particular interaction and improving the underlying model across interactions. A system can already adapt by keeping information in its context or memory. Turning those experiences into reliable improvements in the model is another step, and you have to make sure you’re reinforcing successful behavior rather than just behavior that users happen to respond positively to.

So I’m optimistic about the possibility. But I wouldn’t assume that deployment automatically creates a flywheel. You need to build the machinery that turns experience into useful feedback, and then turns that feedback into better decisions.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about the opportunity, but says deployment does not automatically create a flywheel and emphasizes unresolved requirements. It does not assess the automated flywheel as close to working.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning from deployed experience, but does not identify an existing human-mediated loop where observations of deployed behavior inform changes to that behavior.

r003.rationale: It makes the learning signal central, explaining that interactions alone do not reveal success and that useful feedback should be grounded in observable outcomes of the system’s actions.
